messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am posting this here instead of making a new thread because I have a very similar issue as Laurel did but in opposite form. I have estimated the detection function from pooled duplicate data that occurred during combined double platform effort from dedicated and transit transect legs and now would like to apply it to only my dedicated transect leg data which includes the majority of my detections which occurred on solo primary platform effort. I have 34 total detections on dedicated legs - 10 of which are duplicates that were used to fit the detection function and 24 are from solo primary platform effort.

This is a line transect ship survey for a dolphin species with attractive responsive movement to the boat. My tracker platform was a visual observer team and my primary platform is a towed hydrophone array. I will be applying the mean group size from visual detections to estimate abundance. My current issue is that I cannot find a way to subset either the obs.table or region.table in a way that allows me to apply the detection function from my duplicate data to all of my detections on dedicated legs. I have spent multiple days trying to find a way around this - the best I can do thus far is get dht to create a table with perfect values for area, covered region, effort, and k. For 'n' it only provides the values and cv's of the object ID numbers that were 9 of the 10 duplicates as these were the ones that occurred on dedicated legs. (The 10th was a tracker only sighting and I am not sure if I can include this in my abundance estimate.)

I have 3 survey strata: Region 1 = 8 clusters, Region 2 = 18 clusters, Region 3 = 8 clusters  that were detected on dedicated legs.
This is the closest I have been able to get to the correct output:

It is feasible to be trying to attempt to estimate N in this way? I have been working on calculations of cv's, etc. by hand for all of these data and I would really like to be able to use R or distance software to estimate my cv's for n and N and weighted effort by region for density.

Thus far I have tried a multitude of different ways to subset these data in the dht function. I have tried separating the duplicate data into a second spreadsheet from the dedicated survey effort data and was able to get the above table. I have also been able to get the above table from a single spreadsheet with duplicate and dedicated effort data combined. I have tried renaming my duplicate data to a separate region called 'Dup' and using it to estimate the detection function and then subsetting the remaining regions for the tables that dht calls and this gave me all zeros for 'n'. If possible, can someone please take a look at my attached code and csv and see if you can find a work around for me? This will be massively appreciated!!!

NB* the attached csv file is the combined duplicate and dedicated effort data. Region.Label and Area columns have been modified to reflect 'Dup' named as a region/area in an attempt to subset by region. The original Region.Label and Area columns are the last columns on the spreadsheet.

Thank you,
Morgan Martin

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone! im working on analyzing distance sampling data conducted on two study sites in northern kenya. All species observed were recorded, however I am only interested in giraffe. I seemed to have fit the detection function pretty well (see attached) however my density and abundance estimates are very high, and i'm not sure what is causing it. Below is my code, any help would be greatly appreciated!

giraffe<-data[data$Species=="Giraffe",]
head(giraffe)

region2<-read.csv("region.csv",stringsAsFactors = F)
samples2<-read.csv("samples.csv", stringsAsFactors = F)
obs2<-read.csv("obs.csv",stringsAsFactors = F)

ds.dht.model <- ds(giraffe,.25,region.table=region2,sample.table=samples2,obs.table=obs2)
summary(ds.dht.model)
plot(ds.dht.model)
gof_ds(ds.dht.model)

Hi there,

As Erik said, it's hard to be sure exactly what the problem is with the data you've supplied, but having looked at the output I can't help thinking that units might be part of the issue. Your abundance estimate for the two study areas is 5.5m. I just had a quick look on the internet and found that a recent global estimate for wild populations of giraffe is 97,000. You haven't given units anywhere here, but I imagine that for an animal the size of a giraffe, the X axis of your detection should be in km? I'm just wondering if Distance thinks your distances are specified in metres? If you divide your densities and abundances by 1000000 (to convert from per metre squared to per km squared) then you get approx 55 giraffes over the two areas. Does that sound more sensible?

Best wishes,

Mark

Hi All,

Just want to give an update that my problem has been solved by a friendly distance user! If anyone else runs into this issue please feel free to email me. The issue was resolved through a couple steps in reformatting the csv file: 1) duplicate data used to estimate the detection function contained detections from both dedicated and transit legs. The transit duplicate detections need to be labeled as their own region 'X' and set the area of this region to zero. 2) the single platform primary detections on dedicated legs that were collected when only the primary platform effort was working need to be arranged just like the duplicate data with 2 rows per detection. Here, observer 2 (tracker) will always equal zero and observer 1 will always equal 1. The detected column needs to match this. 3) Lastly, an extra column named whatever you want needs to be added and all rows of duplicate data need to be populated with a 1 and all rows of single platform detections (2 rows per detection) need to be populated with zeros. Treat this column as a factor variable.

Since all of my detections that occurred on dedicated legs when only one effort platform was working happened to occur on the primary platform, the detection function ignored these in the estimate because they were never seen by the tracker. I compared my DF model results using my prior data set up to this one and they are identical. :)  Further, abundance is not estimated for the duplicate detections that occurred on transit legs (Region 'X') and these appear in the final table output as zeros and are not incorporated into the estimates.

My one question that remains regards how to appropriately incorporate the cv of my mean group size value into the cv for D and N. My group size column is only populated with the mean arithmetic group size for all detections (calculated from visual sightings on effort within my truncation distance which are not size biased by distance) thus, my variance is showing up as zero for group size and is not incorporated into my variance estimate. I have selected to estimate the empirical variance for density using Innes et al. 2002 based on an R2 estimator because I am applying the same detection function and group size value to all 3 of my strata. If it is ok to estimate variance based on the delta method for these data please let me know. I am finding the equations to estimate variance for clusters in Marques and Buckland, 2004 quite difficult to follow.

My mean group size = 3.52, se= 0.81, cv = 0.23

This is my current output for D and N in DISTANCE:

Any advice will be much appreciated, I am very happy to be at this stage of the analysis! So close!
Best,
Morgan

messages.subject: Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data
messages.subject_clean: Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am analysing some seabird line transect data using distance methods in R. The data were collected from a ship using standard European Seabirds at Sea Methods (Webb, A. and J. Durinck (1992). Counting birds from ships. Manual for aeroplane and ship surveys of waterfowl and seabirds. IWRB Special Publication. 19: 24-37). In brief, detections are binned at the time of collection into one of four distance bands, bounded by 0-50, 50-100, 100-200 and 200-300 m.

As the data are binned, I planned to assess goodness of fit of potential detection functions using chi-square tests. Eric Rexstad points out in a previous exchange on this list that “degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is defined as u-q-1, where u is the number of bins and q is the number of parameters in the detection function”. With only four bins, I am therefore considered to consider only detection functions containing two or less parameters. However, I have a relatively large sample size (n = 711 clusters). This means that the chi-square test tends to indicate significant discrepancies between my candidate detection functions and the data, an issue that has previously been eluded to here

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distancesampling/chi$20square$20large$20sample%Csort:date/distance-sampling/rf4DlB_ihS4/YIRBQiQnrFMJ

and by Buckland et al. 2015 (section 5.1.4). For example, when I fit a half-normal function with two cosine adjustments to my full data set, the p value for chi-square is 0.006. The same function fitted to a randomly thinned data set of n = 100 results in p = 0.698 for chi-sq.

That being the case, which of the approach to assessing goodness of fit is recommended? (1) Thin the data prior to fitting the detection function and use chi-sq to assess model fit? This seems like a waste of data and would force an arbitrary choice of n. Or (2) use the full data set and simply assess model fit visually, as recommended here:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/degrees$20of$20freedom%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/upAAXToeCVI/x9NKqQlVAQAJ

If approach #2 is preferred, does that mean that it would then be valid to consider models with >2 parameters or should I still constrain my field of candidate models to those with <= 2 parameters (and if so why?!)

Thanks in advance for your assistance.

Ewan Wakefield

messages.body_plain:
Ewan

Glad to see you are paying close attention to model fit diagnostics.  You are correct in all the material you pointed out, with minor exception that the model yuo fitted must have been a half-normal with a *single* adjustment term of order 2 (had it been HN with 2 adjustments you would have a model with 3 parameters, hence no degrees of freedom left for goodness of fit testing).

Your conundrum is how to proceed with GOF testing with binned data with few bins.  This is a matter of some personal preference and others might not agree with my opinion.  I would not use the "random filtering" as it seems artificial.  The purpose of the GOF testing is to assess the validity of the model you are using in the inference you are making about the population estimate.  I would show the reader of your report the chosen detection function superimposed upon the histogram of the data, as produced by the gof_ds() function.  I would also speak to the subject of model fit in your results section, but I would not feel compelled to produce a test statistic in the circumstances you describe.  This is akin to the option (2) you present.

Following on with the second part of your question, conditional upon the adoption of option (2), could you be more expansive in the range of candidate models.  Recognise that option (2) only "buys" you a single degree of freedom, permitting your universe of candidate models to have (perhaps) a half-normal key with 2 adjustments.  I would not expect this to make much practical difference.  In theory we expect detection functions to be fairly smooth, I think it would be unusual for there to be two changes in derivatives (bumps) in a histogram that has only 4 points of support (bins).  That might be over-fitting to the data rather than fitting to the process that gave rise to the data.  I would restrain my enthusiasm for fitting a 3 parameter model to data with 4 points of support, even if I was not constrained to "saving" a degree of freedom for testing of fit.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your constructive reply, Eric.

>with minor exception that the model yuo fitted must have been a half-normal with a *single* adjustment term of order 2

Correct - that was a typo. In the first instance, I also fitted a uniform function with two cosine adjustments; a half-normal with one Hermite polynomial adjustment; and a hazard rate function with no adjustments. The latter has the lowest AIC and best fit according to the chi-sq test.

>Following on with the second part of your question, conditional upon the adoption of option (2), could you be more expansive in the range of candidate models.

In addition to the candidate models described above, exploratory analysis suggests that a whole suite of covariates affect the rate of decay of the detection function. These include sea state and wind speed (which are obviously colinear so I wouldn't consider both in the same model), cluster size and observer. Based on your reply, it seems reasonable that I could consider a half-normal model (with no adjustments) and parameters for wind speed (or sea state) and cluster size, as well as sub-models contained therein.  Observer has eight levels so I presume that this there's no way that this covaraite could also be considered. Am I right that the only option for capturing variation due to observer with my data set would be stratify by observer? Presumably, the alternative would be to trust that pooling robustness deals with inter-observer variability?

All the best,

Ewan

The purpose of the GOF testing is to assess the validity of the model you are using in the inference you are making about the population estimate.  I would show the reader of your report the chosen detection function superimposed upon the histogram of the data, as produced by the gof_ds() function.  I would also speak to the subject of model fit in your results section, but I would not feel compelled to produce a test statistic in the circumstances you describe.  This is akin to the option (2) you present.
>
> Following on with the second part of your question, conditional upon the adoption of option (2), could you be more expansive in the range of candidate models. I would not expect this to make much practical difference.  In theory we expect detection functions to be fairly smooth, I think it would be unusual for there to be two changes in derivatives (bumps) in a histogram that has only 4 points of support (bins).  That might be over-fitting to the data rather than fitting to the process that gave rise to the data. messages.subject: Distance sampling surveys targeting multiple taxa
messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling surveys targeting multiple taxa
messages.body_plain:
Hi list,
I have been wondering how much influence survey design is likely to have on the power and accuracy of distance sampling surveys. More specifically, how many species are too many to survey for?
For example, ship-based distance sampling surveys collecting data on cetaceans are widely accepted as being one of the best methods for estimating abundance. However, what would happen to the data if more target species were added to these surveys? If seabirds were also recorded, would the detection probability decrease as observers are looking for multiple cue types simultaneously?

Similarly, I was wondering if recorded numbers of one taxa and accuracy may decline due to surveyors counting a flock of birds when dolphins were passing by, leaving less time to count them and collect accurate bearings etc? I suppose this would depend upon the density of animals in the area, but I'm imagining a feeding flock scenario that is also attended by dolphins or whales.

On a smaller-scale, is there any merit collecting data on a single target species as opposed to a family or order? Say for example if a survey was collecting data on fin whales, is there any evidence that the data would be better than if observers collected data on all cetaceans? I wonder if a bit of variety and more frequent sightings (within reason) may keep observers awake!

I'm interested to hear your thoughts, and if there have been any studies looking into this then it would be great to be directed towards them.
Many thanks,
James

messages.body_plain:
James

You raise good questions, but I don't know there are concrete answers to them (how many species are too many?).  It stands to reason that deterioration in observer performance will occur as the numbr of target species increases.  I've done a quick scan of our distance sampling bibliography (http://distancesampling.org/dbib.html) and have not found any information exactly on point.

I would expect that a simulated situation would be needed to induce a multi-species situation and ascertain the change in detectability caused by differing number of individuals or species.  While not pertinent to cetacean or seabird studies, researchers at North Carolina State Univ built an outdoor "bird radio" laboratory.  They published a number of papers addressing detectability issues associated with ambient noise and multiple species, not only upon detectability but also accuracy distance measurements.  Perhaps something in those papers might be useful to you.

Alldredge, M. W., Simons, T. R. & Pollock, K. H., 2007. Factors affecting aural detections of songbirds.
Ecological Applications 17:948--955   http://doi.wiley.com/10.1890/06-0685

The issue of observer swamping can be compensated to some extent by having a field protocol calling for observer behaviour to change in the presence of high animal densities.  There also needs to be elements of the protocol prioritising the "target species".

This may be a subject our field biologist readers might lend an opinion.

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

These are questions that are frequently asked in the field ( during those long hours spent staring at empty sea) but I'm not aware of anyone having addressed them analytically.

> However, what would happen to the data if more target species were added to these surveys? If seabirds were also recorded, would the detection probability decrease as observers are looking for multiple cue types simultaneously?

During the Scans II survey, at least one ship had both seabird and cetacean observers working simultaneously (but on different platforms). The bird observer recorded cetaceans as well as seabirds. I heard at the time that these data were going to be analysed to see if cetacean abundance estimates made using data collected using the ESAS survey method were similar to those made using dedicated cetacean surveys. I'm not sure if this analysis ever happened - someone from SMRU would know. If not, the data should be there to analyse...

>
> Similarly, I was wondering if recorded numbers of one taxa and accuracy may decline due to surveyors counting a flock of birds when dolphins were passing by, leaving less time to count them and collect accurate bearings etc? I suppose this would depend upon the density of animals in the area, but I'm imagining a feeding flock scenario that is also attended by dolphins or whales.

This can definitely be an issue during ESAS-style surveys. As James suggests, a clear protocol goes some way to standardising data collection is such scenarios. Experienced surveyors tend to be be better at keeping a cool head when confronted with big muti-species feeding aggregations. In terms of analysis, one could consider association with other species as a covariate. In fact, I've just been looking at this and some small seabirds definitely become more detectable when they're associated with other seabirds or cetaceans.

>
> On a smaller-scale, is there any merit collecting data on a single target species as opposed to a family or order? Say for example if a survey was collecting data on fin whales, is there any evidence that the data would be better than if observers collected data on all cetaceans? I wonder if a bit of variety and more frequent sightings (within reason) may keep observers awake!

On most ship-based surveys, multi-species groups of cetaceans occur so infrequently that there's little chance of missing one species because observers are focused on another. That said, a potential issue with primary platform observers is that they can spend so long looking at one animal, that they miss others in the vicinity. This sometimes happens with Mysticetes because observers try to identify each animal to species. Again, a good field protocol can minimise the chances of this resulting in missing animals on the line. e.g. a second observer could be dedicated to identifying animals, perhaps using digital photography, once the first observer has detected them. Double-platform techniques can also be used to used to assess the proportion of animals missed on the track line but it's probably better not to miss them in the first place, if possible.

Regards,

Ewan
